## Principle

Heat exchangers are among the most widely used items of equipment in the whole of process engineering, and a clear understanding of how they work is essential for any engineer involved in thermal design. In essence, heat passes from a hot stream to a cold stream through the wall that separates them, and the rate at which this transfer takes place is governed by three key factors: the area of the wall, the overall heat transfer coefficient, and the temperature difference between the two streams. It is important to note that the temperature difference is by no means constant along the length of an exchanger. Each stream changes temperature as it gives up or takes in heat, which means that the local difference at one end generally differs from the local difference at the other end, thereby making it necessary either to build the duty up from local rates or to adopt a suitable mean difference for design purposes.

Furthermore, two flow arrangements bound the behaviour of the unit. In countercurrent flow, the streams move in opposite directions, so that the hot inlet faces the cold outlet and the temperature difference remains comparatively even from end to end; remarkably, a temperature cross is possible under this arrangement, meaning that the cold stream can leave hotter than the hot stream leaves. In cocurrent flow, by contrast, the streams enter at the same end, the inlet difference is the largest in the unit, and the difference decays progressively along the length as the two streams approach a common temperature which, as a matter of principle, they cannot pass.

An energy balance written on each stream ties the duty to the temperature change experienced by that stream, and the two balances must, of course, agree on one and the same duty. The log-mean temperature difference serves as the constant difference which, when multiplied by the area and the overall coefficient, returns the true duty, provided that the coefficient is constant and the temperature changes follow the balance. For its part, the overall coefficient conveniently bundles together the resistances of the two fluid films and the wall into a single figure, while the film on each side depends on how fast and how turbulently that side happens to flow.

## Equipment

The shell-and-tube exchanger, which is widely regarded as the workhorse of the industry, carries one stream inside a bundle of tubes and the other around the bundle inside a shell. Baffles fold the shell-side path back and forth across the tubes, raising the velocity and, with it, the film coefficient, and the tube side may make several passes through the shell. This robust and versatile type tolerates high pressure and high temperature, and the bundle can be withdrawn for cleaning, although these advantages come at the cost of a large and heavy unit.

The plate exchanger, meanwhile, stacks thin corrugated plates with gaskets between them, and the two streams occupy alternate channels. The passages are narrow and the flow in them becomes turbulent at modest rates, so the unit is pleasingly compact and the coefficient high; however, the gaskets limit the pressure and temperature that the stack can hold, and the pack opens up for cleaning, which makes it well suited to duties where fouling is frequent and mild.

The air-cooled exchanger rejects heat to air blown over finned tubes. The fins generously extend the air-side area, on the side where the film coefficient is poor, and the type removes the need for cooling water altogether, which is valuable where water is scarce or expensive, at the cost of a large plot area and a cold-stream outlet temperature that follows the weather. Last but not least, the double-pipe exchanger, consisting simply of one pipe inside another, serves small duties and high pressures with simple construction and little area per unit length.

Overall, the choice among the types turns on pressure, temperature, the fouling tendency of the streams, and the cleaning that the unit will need in service. No type escapes the wall and the two films; the types differ essentially in how the area is packed and how the unit is opened, cleaned, and repaired.

## Worked example

As an illustrative example, consider a hot liquid stream that is to be cooled by water in a countercurrent unit, for which the required area is to be determined. First of all, the duty is taken from the energy balance on the hot stream: the duty is the heat that the stream gives up between its inlet and outlet temperatures. The duty is then checked against the balance on the water side, where exactly the same duty appears as the heat the water takes in between its own inlet and outlet, since the two balances describe one single transfer and must therefore return the same figure, highlighting the internal consistency of the approach.

Next, the terminal differences are found from the four stream temperatures. At the hot end, the entering hot stream faces the leaving water, while at the cold end the cooled stream faces the entering water. The hot-end difference turns out to be the larger of the two here, because the water leaves warm while the hot stream enters at its hottest. The log-mean of the two terminal differences is then adopted as the driving force. The log-mean lies between the two terminal values, nearer to the smaller one where the ends differ widely, and it is precisely the difference that the rate equation requires.

The duty is divided by the product of the overall coefficient and the log-mean difference in order to obtain the area. The result is checked in two ways. The log-mean difference falls between the terminal differences, as any respectable mean must, and the area comes out larger than the area a cocurrent unit would need only if the cocurrent mean difference were the larger, which it is not: the cocurrent arrangement allows the difference to collapse along the length, its mean is smaller, and it consequently needs the larger area for the same duty. The calculation therefore sizes the countercurrent unit, and the comparison neatly shows what the flow arrangement is worth.

## Limits

It must be emphasised that the simple model rests on a constant overall coefficient, and the coefficient is constant only where the fluid properties and the flow regimes hold steady along the unit. A stream whose viscosity changes sharply with temperature, or a stream that boils or condenses over part of the area, moves the coefficient from section to section, and a single mean difference then misstates the local driving force, so that the unit has to be rated in sections instead.

Moreover, fouling introduces an additional resistance that grows steadily in service, so the coefficient used by the model on the first day is not the coefficient of a year later, and any area chosen with no fouling margin inevitably falls short before the first cleaning. Multipass and crossflow arrangements fall short of the true countercurrent difference, and their mean difference is the countercurrent log-mean reduced by a correction factor that depends on the arrangement and the temperature changes. In cocurrent flow, the outlet temperatures cannot cross, which effectively caps the heat recovery that the arrangement can achieve regardless of how much area is provided. In conclusion, the model is best regarded as a sizing estimate: it returns the area that a stated duty requires under stated assumptions, and it says nothing about whether the streams, once distributed through a real unit, will actually meet those assumptions.
